profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a regional digital health research consortium evaluating a draft protocol for applying a standardized health technology assessment framework to three upcoming eHealth pilot services: a COPD remote monitoring app, an asynchronous dermatology teleconsult platform, and a hospital discharge chatbot. The draft protocol is intended to operationalize insights from a systematic review on eHealth HTA frameworks into a reusable review template for partner hospitals. The agenda is to assess whether the protocol is 'review-ready' for circulation to pilot sites, check whether the proposed stepped assessment approach and reporting template are sufficiently specified, and decide what revisions are needed before sending the package to the consortium steering group next week. The expected outcome is agreement to move forward with a revised protocol package and a short list of edits each person will complete.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hoffmann
members.role: Senior Health Economist and HTA Method Lead
members.expertise: Health technology assessment methodology, economic evaluation, comparative evidence synthesis, hospital adoption frameworks
members.background: Lena leads methodological work packages in EU-funded digital health projects and previously worked at a national HTA agency adapting assessment templates for non-drug interventions.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol approved with minimal restructuring because the steering group expects a near-final methods package, and she is especially concerned that the framework look rigorous and comparable across sites.
hidden_assumptions: A 'stepped approach' means an initial cross-site screening layer followed by optional deeper modules only if a service clears that first gate.
'Reporting characteristics' refers primarily to the standardized service-description fields in the main template, not to implementation context appendices.

If the protocol is 'review-ready,' then core methodological logic, decision rules, and minimum documentation fields are stable enough for external circulation even if examples and annex formatting are still incomplete.
The 'pilot sites' discussed in the draft are the three live services scheduled for Q3 deployment, not retrospective case examples used during framework testing.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Digital Health Implementation Scientist and Clinical Workflow Lead
members.expertise: Implementation evaluation, service redesign, clinician workflow integration, pragmatic digital health pilots
members.background: Arjun has led rollout evaluations for telehealth and patient engagement tools across two hospital networks and often translates research frameworks into operational checklists for frontline teams.
members.private_state: He wants the protocol to remain usable for site coordinators and worries that an overly abstract HTA process will fail in practice if context and workflow variation are not captured up front.
hidden_assumptions: A 'stepped approach' means staged evidence collection over time within each service, starting lean before implementation and adding more dimensions after real-world use begins.
'Reporting characteristics' naturally includes workflow, staffing, interoperability constraints, and local service configuration details, even if those appear in appendices.
If the protocol is 'review-ready,' site teams should be able to apply it without major interpretation and without needing a methods call to fill in practical gaps.
The 'pilot sites' under discussion include the two retrospective demonstration cases already mapped in workshop materials, since those are part of proving applicability before rollout.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the protocol should use a 'stepped approach' tailored to functional characteristics.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a tiered assessment architecture: every service gets a common first-pass screen, and only selected services move into deeper HTA modules.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a time-phased assessment pathway within each service: start with a lightweight pre-implementation assessment and add fuller evaluation once the service is in use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the review language and sounds canonically correct to both; because both support tailoring and sequencing, each hears confirmation of their own familiar interpretation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the package needs standardized 'reporting characteristics' for each eHealth service.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this covers the core descriptive metadata in the main HTA template: target population, intervention function, comparator, setting, maturity level, and intended outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this also includes operational context details such as staffing model, escalation workflow, local EHR integration, procurement constraints, and training burden.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see these details as obviously part of describing a service, but they mentally place them in different parts of the package; the shared umbrella phrase masks the boundary difference.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the protocol is almost 'review-ready' for circulation next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'review-ready' means the methodological core is fixed enough for steering-group feedback, even if examples, guidance notes, and some annexes are unfinished.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'review-ready' means a pilot-site coordinator could realistically use the package as-is with only minor cosmetic edits.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'review-ready' often functions as a reassuring progress marker rather than a formally defined gate, so both can agree on the phrase while applying different adequacy standards.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the framework has enough evidence from the 'pilot sites' to show applicability.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the three prospective Q3 deployment services named in the protocol cover note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is including those three plus two earlier retrospective demonstration cases from an internal workshop deck.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have recently worked on materials that used the same phrase, and the retrospective cases are familiar enough to feel like part of the same pilot portfolio without anyone restating the list.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this moving toward approval. For next week's steering-group circulation, 'review-ready' means the core methodological architecture is stable: screening layer, decision logic, minimum fields, and enough wording discipline that it looks rigorous across sites. We do not need to hold this up because annex examples and formatting are still rough.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I suggest we keep today focused on two things: whether the draft protocol is almost review-ready for circulation next week, and whether the standardized template is reflecting what came through from the systematic review in a sufficiently coherent way.

turns.inner_thought: Close, yes, but only if a site coordinator can actually pick this up and run with it. If people still need a methods call to understand the flow, then it's not really review-ready in any practical sense. And when we say pilot sites, I'm thinking of the full spread we've already worked through, including the earlier demonstration cases, because that's where usability issues showed up.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the main test is practical applicability across the pilot sites. The package looks close if site teams can follow the assessment flow without much interpretation and see how it applies in real settings.

turns.inner_thought: The stepped approach is the backbone here: everyone gets the same first-pass screen, and only then do we move selected services into deeper modules. That's what gives us comparability and prevents every site from improvising a full assessment from day one.
turns.utterance: On the methods side, I do think the stepped approach is the right structure. It gives us a disciplined first pass across services while still leaving room for additional depth where that's warranted.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: start light before rollout so sites don't disengage, then build the assessment in stages once real-world use starts generating evidence. That's the only way this will remain workable for frontline teams under time pressure.
turns.utterance: I agree, the stepped approach is probably the only realistic way to keep this usable. If we start lean and then build out the assessment as the service matures, I think sites will stay engaged rather than seeing it as an upfront burden.

turns.inner_thought: The main template just needs the service-description fields cleaned up so each site enters the same core metadata: population, function, comparator, setting, maturity, outcomes. If those reporting characteristics are tidy, the package will already look much stronger.
turns.utterance: For me, the main remaining edit is tightening the reporting characteristics table so each eHealth service is described in a standardized and comparable way across the consortium.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and those reporting characteristics have to include the operational realities people trip over: who owns the workflow, where handoffs happen, integration dependencies, escalation pathways, staffing and training load. Otherwise the template will look neat but miss what determines whether a site can actually use it.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. If we're standardizing reporting characteristics, I'd just want to make sure the description is rich enough to support implementation as well, so sites can complete it consistently and not leave out the details that matter in practice.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want this to turn into another request for more case material. The three live services are enough to show applicability at this stage; the steering group mainly needs confidence that the structure is sound. If we keep reopening examples, we'll lose the timeline.
turns.utterance: On applicability, I think we've already shown enough through the pilot sites for this stage. What the steering group really needs now is confidence in the protocol structure, rather than a larger set of illustrations.

turns.inner_thought: I agree there's enough spread because, taken together, the current pilots plus the earlier demonstration cases already show the framework can travel across different workflows. That's actually reassuring to me; it means we don't need to invent more examples, just make better use of the ones we've got.
turns.utterance: I think that's fair. The pilot sites already give us a decent spread, and between the dermatology and chatbot work and the earlier examples we've discussed, it does show the framework travels reasonably well.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then we can keep the package lean for circulation: core protocol, the template, and the module decision logic. Worked examples and polished annexes can wait. As long as the methodological spine is in place, it's review-ready enough for steering-group feedback.
turns.utterance: In that case, I'd propose we send the core protocol, the template, and the decision logic next week, and treat the fuller worked examples and annex refinements as a later version rather than a blocker now.

turns.inner_thought: That should work if I add some brief user-facing guidance. Coordinators will need help applying the stepped approach in practice and knowing how to fill in the reporting characteristics without guessing. If I can make that explicit, the package may actually be usable even if some of the annexes come later.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can work with that. I'll add a short guidance layer so coordinators can apply the stepped approach and complete the reporting characteristics more consistently at site level.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll clean the core template and keep the methods language tight. He can strengthen the applicability notes linked to the pilot sites, but I want that framed as supportive context, not an invitation to reopen the structure. We need this out next week.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll take the template cleanup and align the wording across the core sections. Could you strengthen the applicability notes tied to the pilot sites before we circulate, just so that piece reads a bit more confidently?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that gives me room to make the package clearer for actual rollout while still hitting the review deadline. If I sharpen the guidance and applicability notes, then from my perspective it should be ready both for next week's review and for sites to start using soon after.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. With those edits in place, I think the package should be in good shape for next week's review and then practical rollout afterward.
